en: If that is too little, let me shed
All my blood as well.
Let me open my treasury's mouth,
Let me scatter my wealth.
Such is the command God has sent;
Let me accept it as it is.
To all four corners of the world,
Let me send precise word.
The Muslims throughout the earth—
Let me gather them all.
The suffering people have spoken of this;
Let me agree to their words.
For those who have heard his fame,
Let me hold magnanimous Manas's memorial feast.
For the foolish and feeble-minded,
Let me hold a celebration for my son.
The eight khans upon the earth—
Let me gather them all.
Let me send word to my people.
Gathering the peoples of eight khans,
Holding horse races and a feast,
Devising a thoughtful plan,
Let me send firm word to my people.
Let me gather the peoples of eight khans,
And not stand idly by.
Placing my golden crown upon him,
Seating him on a golden throne,
Let me give my people a spectacle.
This dear lad, gained after such hardship—
Let me raise him as khan over my people.
When he becomes the people's father,
Will he give up his unruliness?
When he becomes the people's master,
Will he give up his oppression?
When he becomes the people's leader,
Will this orphan abandon his violence?"
Saying this, Temir Khan
Sent word to his people,
To all the populace.
The news rang out loudly
Through the walled city of Bukhara.
On the marsh of Üyrülmö
They gathered for an assembly.
On the marsh of Chogulma
They came together.
They settled on weighty counsel,
And held a great assembly.
Choosing thoroughbreds and giving mounts,
To all the various khans
He sent letters without fail.
When Temir Khan gave the order,
They took six swift horses,
And letters the size of a palm.
To the four corners of the world
They delivered the news in full.
To the five corners of the known world
They sent firm word.
Dwelling in Sary-Arka,
A weighty, formidable hero, they said;
Dwelling in broad Sary-Arka,
An imposing hero, they said;
Who husked his millet, stones and all;
When they bellowed out their songs,
No elder stayed at home;
Who defended foul-mouthed talk,
Who praised his wife like a maiden;
With watery sour milk and lean dried curds,
With wooden lattice walls,
Descended from their forefather Alach—
Hero Kökchö, Aydarkan's son,
And Ümötöy, Kökchö's son—
He came eagerly from the Kazakhs.
The mounts of all of them
Were all swift dun horses,
With amulet-shaped forehead marks,
All outstanding steeds.
He came to race his horse.
Dwelling in Jelpinish,
A son of the seven Kyrgyz tribes,
My golden-crowned Muzburchak—
Muzburchak's Burambek
Came to race his horse.
Wearing coats of blue iron,
Riding blue and reddish gray horses,
Their hair-tails tied in tight knots;
Riding tireless Karabayyr horses,
With sieve-like lungs and copper limbs,
Horses akin to unseen spirits;
Their banners, swords, and spears
Made ready at their waists;
Each with a dagger
Fastened at his waist;
Dwelling in lower Chambyl-Bel,
A bold and capable people, they said;
All wearing splendid coats,
Tall of body, broad of shoulder,
Falling upon the foes they faced,
Prepared for battle from their earliest days;
Their faces like buttered wheat,
With beauty unlike other people's;
Their swords fitting snugly,
With hats like leather pails on their heads;
Never shrinking a hair's breadth from death,
Never having someone carry slander—
Janaaly of Chambyl-Bel
Came to race his horse.
The great holy city of sheikhs,
The multitude of Kokand and Margilan—
Kozubek of the Khan of Kokand
Came to race his horse.
Malabek from Margilan
Came to race his horse.
Ruling Andijan,
Fork-bearded Synchybek
Came to race his horse.
Dwelling in Six Cities and Kashgar,
Upward-bearded Özübek
Came to race his horse.
Eight khans came side by side.
The people of four khans were all Sarts.
As though these were too few,
They came from lower Hindustan as well.
Though the people swarmed together,
Still more were on the road.
From Six Cities and Andijan,
Many had no saddles;
Still more rode on saddle pads.
The arrivals had no sense.
Was it a custom left by their fathers?
The white saddles of Andijan
Had no cruppers at all.
Keeping their whips at the ready,
If they had but a single horse,
They kept it as a stallion.
The people of Six Cities formed a group apart,
Their blue overshoes sticking out.
For those who knew, it was Khan Manas's memorial feast;
For those who did not, it was Semetey's celebration.
They celebrated with horse races;
The peoples of the world assembled.
On the uplands of broad Bukhara,
With seven hundred households under her hand,
Kanykey, reigning there,
Heard news from the arrivals:
The peoples of eight khans had gathered;
She heard they would hold a horse race.
When she heard this news,
Taking the courser Taytoru,
Your sister-in-law sought a good omen.
She fed him barnyard millet from the rice,
And sweated him every day.
She hung up a bag of barley feed,
And sweated him each month.
The gray belt left by Manas
She fitted snugly round her neck.
To God, whose command is mighty,
She sobbed and pleaded,
Her rib bones seeming to break,
Tears pouring from her eyes.
All her thoughts were scattered;
Her breast could not contain her cares.
Buried world, may you come to no good!
Your sister-in-law's tears streamed in ten directions.
From her dear quail-like eyes
Tears fell in separate drops.
From her dear currant-like eyes
Tears streamed a whip's length.
"Allah, God the Creator,
I have been left here alone.
I have no support to lean on,
No secure place of my own.
Saying, 'It is our sister-in-law's horse,'
If I race Taytoru for the prize,
To urge him on more strongly,
My former Kyrgyz people are not here.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Were you always like this, shitty world?
If I race Taytoru,
He was a very swift creature.
When my valiant lord died,
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
My dear uncle,
Gave him as a funeral gift.
When I counted his years of maturity,
He had reached sixty.
This very year, my Taytoru
Had reached sixty years of maturity.
Who would show affection
To a widow like me?
Let me race him to divine my fate,
This swift horse of mine, Taytoru.
If Taytoru comes in front,
Of this Bukhara here
Let me share out the highest prize.
If Taytoru falls behind,
Rather than be called a shameless woman,
Let me die before my appointed death.
If Taytoru comes through,
Let me unburden the sorrow within me.
If Taytoru does not come through,
The black blood in my heart
Let me scatter over the open steppe.
If he is a lion taking after his father,
If he is a hero who shakes the world,
If I can take my migrating camp from Keng-Kol,
On that imposing wretch
If I can take my revenge;
If I can take my migrating camp from Talas,
On that swaggering wretch
If I live to take my revenge;
If things become as they once were,
If God settles me in Talas,
My people, who beg for drink and are never full,
Who never abandon their greed,
My sovereign Kyrgyz people—
If God lets me see them again,
My horse Taytoru, come through!
If all I grasp is burning coals,
If the courage of this son of mine
Does not equal his father's,
My horse Taytoru, fall behind!
If all I grasp is burning coals,
If the courage of this son of mine
Does not equal his father's,
If Taytoru falls behind,
Let me die before my appointed death.
If Taytoru comes in front,
Of this Bukhara here
Let me scatter the prize abroad.
Wretched world, what can I do?
My forehead bone was sloping;
When the hero passed away,
I had few days left to live.
What I dug was pitch-dark night.
When my khan passed away,
It was such a terrible day.
Wandering back to her own kin,
This fierce woman's forehead bore thick misfortune.
The death of my noble lord—
Will it ever leave my very bones?
The torment I, unfortunate, suffered,
When they found their chance against me;
It has not left my very bones,
How that wretched dog slashed my breast.
Wearing felt socks, without overshoes,
This wretched soul grieves.
Wearing felt socks, without boots,
This wretched soul finds dying hard.
What I dug became a dreadful pit;
What I saw became utter misfortune.
That dear bird, the wild duck,
Flies without turning back, seeking the steppe.
How much I, poor soul, endured,
For the child born from my womb!
The countless riches left by the Slayer—
How can I forget scattering them?
